extracted.intended_audience: students and teachers of poetry and literary criticism; aspiring critics and informed general readers
extracted.subtask_description: Guidelines for reading and evaluating lyric and short poems, emphasizing avoidance of stock responses and sentimentality, and judging a poem by its own internal features. Focuses on how readers' habits, experience, and preconceptions affect interpretation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid initial prepossession (reader bias)
rubrics_metrics.description: The critic must guard against an initial prepossession—the desire to find grounds for approval or condemnation—which often takes charge of the whole process.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Read with a major interest in reading faithfully; be watchful that a prior wish to like or dislike does not control interpretation. Note instances where readers 'want to read a poem in a certain way' and thereby misread. Example anti-pattern: deciding a poem is 'bad' before attending to its actual details.

rubrics_metrics.name: Recognise and resist stock responses
rubrics_metrics.description: Stock responses—prepackaged rhythms, images, sentiments, or ideas imported into the reading—can distort a passage and replace what the poem actually develops.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Identify where familiarity, conventional images, or standard emotional reactions are filling gaps or overriding the poem's particulars (e.g., stock image of a cloud, stock notion of an epitaph). Check whether each item of meaning and cadence is genuinely in the poem or borrowed from a cultural repertory. Compare with more individuated poems (e.g., Donne) to detect impersonality.

rubrics_metrics.name: Judge the poem by its own internal standards
rubrics_metrics.description: No poem can be judged by standards external to itself; evaluation should focus on what the poem is as itself rather than how it conforms to outside models.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use internal evidence—tone, sequence of feeling, phrasing, formal movements—rather than imposing external expectations. Comparative examples are legitimate only as a means of highlighting features, not as external yardsticks.

rubrics_metrics.name: Assess appropriateness of stock responses to situation
rubrics_metrics.description: Stock responses must be judged by (a) their appropriateness to the situations to which they reply and (b) the degree to which they hinder more appropriate responses from developing.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Distinguish between stock responses that are serviceable and those that obstruct deeper or more fitting reactions. Good stock responses: 'right as far as they go' and help further development; bad ones: inappropriate and powerful enemies to poetry.

rubrics_metrics.name: Evaluate individuality versus impersonality
rubrics_metrics.description: Extreme impersonality—absence of personal individual character in movement or phrasing—signals composition from stock responses rather than a distinctive authorial voice.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Look for personal twists, unique phrasing, idiosyncratic movements (contrast with Donne's Sonnet). If a poem's touches are merely echoes of other poets or 'might well have been written by a committee,' treat impersonality as evidence of facility/stockness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinguish native familiarity from acquired familiarity
rubrics_metrics.description: Familiarity that belongs to a poem as first encountered (native) suggests it arises from stock mental movements and facility; in contrast, acquired familiarity (through repeated reading) is different and compatible with great poetry.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ask whether the poem's familiarity would surprise a fresh attentive reader. Native immediate predictability indicates stock composition; acquired familiarity that still yields surprises is characteristic of great poems.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consider popularity and accessibility cautiously
rubrics_metrics.description: A poem's ease of reception and popularity (coming 'home to a majority of readers with minimum trouble') is not by itself a proof of value; accessibility may indicate stock responses but can also be harmless or useful.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not equate immediate popular appeal with poetic worth; examine whether ease comes from appropriate common responses or from superficiality that prevents further development.

rubrics_metrics.name: Account for reader's experience and background
rubrics_metrics.description: Readers' withdrawal from experience (physical, moral, conventional, intellectual) fosters ill-appropriate, stereotyped reactions; a critic must assess how a reader's background shapes interpretation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider a reader's exposure to relevant experience (e.g., country/sea, moral breadth) and intellectual habits. Recognise that limited or specialised experience can make responses parasitic on ideas rather than particulars.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinguish ideas (representations) from direct experience
rubrics_metrics.description: An 'idea' is a representation that is both less than and more than the object—it is sketchy and coloured by feelings; critics should prefer responses rooted in experience rather than mere ideas.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be suspicious of interpretations based on ready-made ideas or clichés that lack reference to particular sensory or experiential detail. Use poems to test and reorganise inadequate ideas; favour grounded, experience-based readings.

rubrics_metrics.name: Be aware of transmission and communication effects
rubrics_metrics.description: Mass transmission (cinema, press, teachers) tends to standardise and level down ideas and responses; the economics of communication favour crude, widely transmittable responses over subtle ones.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When evaluating recurring stock elements, consider whether they are products of cultural transmission and loss in successive handings. Expect a tendency toward standardisation and be alert to its effects on poetic taste.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use contact with reality as corrective
rubrics_metrics.description: The corrective to inappropriate stock responses is closer contact with reality—direct experience or mediated through other minds and good poetry.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Encourage readings informed by diverse experience and serious engagement with poems that force reorganisation of responses. Treat poetry as a repository of standards that can help break up unreal ideas and responses.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sentimentality — quantitative sense (excessive emotion)
rubrics_metrics.description: A response is sentimental in the quantitative sense when emotions are 'too easily stirred' or too great for the occasion—the flood-gates of emotion are raised excessively.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Judge emotional intensity relative to the situational warrant. Consider extraneous facilitators (drugs, fatigue, mass suggestion) that may make emotions facile. Do not call a poem sentimental without assessing whether the emotion is proportionate to the occasion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sentimentality — qualitative sense (crude vs refined emotion)
rubrics_metrics.description: A response is sentimental in the qualitative sense when it is crude—applying broadly to many situations—rather than refined—sensitive to narrow situational differences.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess whether the emotion is a blunt generality (crude) or a subtle, discriminating reaction (refined). Crude emotions are less likely to be precisely appropriate; refinement can achieve greater appropriateness but is more error-prone.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sentimentality — persistence/sentiment sense (inappropriate due to entrenched dispositions)
rubrics_metrics.description: A response is sentimental when, through over-persistence of tendencies or interaction of sentiments, it becomes inappropriate—confined to one aspect or substituting a factitious situation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examine whether past dispositions ('sentiments' as organised tendencies) are determining present reaction regardless of the actual situation. Look for responses shaped by old habits that misrepresent or flatten the poem's situation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinguish where sentimentality originates (author vs reader)
rubrics_metrics.description: When accusing a poem of sentimentality, distinguish whether the poem's author produced it from a sentimentally disposed mind or whether the critic/reader is being sentimental in responding.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Separate claims about authorship (the poem is the product of a sentimental mind) from claims about reception (the reader would be sentimental to accept the poem uncritically). Avoid conflating authorial intent with reader susceptibility.

rubrics_metrics.name: Detect artifice where expression precedes feeling
rubrics_metrics.description: If formal conveniences (antithesis, rhyme, mechanical structure) indicate that facility of expression has led feeling rather than feeling dictating expression, the poem may be sentimental or manufactured.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Look for signs that rhetoric, neatness, or compositional tricks are being used to elicit emotion rather than arise from genuine situational feeling. Example: antitheses praised in one protocol passage but elsewhere producing dislike suggest mechanical manufacture of effect.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinguish stock responses that enable depth from those that merely mimic feeling
rubrics_metrics.description: Some stock responses are admirable and assist deeper responses (e.g., Gray's Elegy uses stock churchyard responses but also contains Gray's peculiarities); others draw out only superficial feeling and deceive readers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Determine whether the poem uses familiar responses as a foundation for distinctive personal development or whether it merely stimulates predictable reactions without deeper content. Re-reading and attentive comparison can reveal deception.
